source: Kounios et al. (2006) The prepared mind: neural activity prior to problem presentation predicts subsequent solution by sudden insight (Exp 1, EEG)
finding: Brain state in the 2 s before a problem appears predicts whether the next solution will be by insight. Insight preparation had less low-alpha (9-10 Hz) power over mid-frontal cortex. Non-insight preparation had less 8-9 Hz alpha over occipital cortex.
numbers: Exp 1: 19 participants, 186 CRA problems, 30 s limit. Solved 46.2% (SD 8.2). 56.2% of solutions labelled insight (SD 8.3, median RT 7.70 s), 42.5% noninsight (7.48 s). 11.5% of responses were errors.
quote: Effects were also found in the gamma band (>30 Hz), but could not be reliably distinguished from electromyograph artifact
limits: Small N. Topographic EEG, self-report labels. Authors say the gamma-band effects could not be reliably distinguished from electromyograph artifact and were not reported. This is the earliest admission that EMG is a threat to scalp gamma claims in this paradigm.
agent_relevance: Pre-problem state matters, but it is a human brain-state effect with no direct model analogue. Weak analogy: the preparation set (broad vs focused) before a problem could be a prompt-level choice.

source: Kounios et al. (2006) The prepared mind (Exp 2, fMRI)
finding: Same preparation effect found with fMRI. Rest interval before an insight solution showed more activity in anterior cingulate, posterior cingulate and bilateral posterior middle/superior temporal gyri than before a noninsight solution.
numbers: Exp 2: 25 participants after 5 replaced, 135 CRA problems, 15 s limit. Solved 47% (SD 9.9); 55.8% insight (SD 13.9, median RT 5.84 s), 43.4% noninsight (7.81 s). 6.6% errors. Second-stage threshold t(24) = 3.374, p < 0.0025 combined with a cluster size rule.
limits: Same lab, same task family; this is an internal convergence check, not an independent replication. Small clusters; some temporal clusters were driven by decreases in noninsight preparation. Anterior temporal clusters were not significant.
agent_relevance: Convergence across EEG and fMRI makes a pre-problem state plausible, but it still counts as one source. Nothing to measure in a model at inference.

source: Bowden and Jung-Beeman (2003) Aha! Insight experience correlates with solution activation in the right hemisphere. Psychon Bull Rev 10:730-737
finding: Behavioural, not neural. After unsolved CRA problems, solution words rated as insightful were primed more than ones not rated insightful, and this link was stronger for words shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere). Authors state both hemispheres contribute; RH holds weak solution activation.
numbers: N = 44. Problems attempted for 7 s, then naming, solution decision, insight rating 1-5. Unsolved trials: priming 70 ms lvf-RH vs 39 ms rvf-LH; RH advantage 33 ms, F(1,43)=4.4, p=.04. Solved trials: priming 106 ms lvf-RH vs 48 ms rvf-LH. Within-rating lvf-RH advantage about 40 ms (rating 5) and 63 ms (rating 4); test values in the extracted text were garbled, so not recorded. Correlation z' about .18 (lvf) vs .05 (rvf), t(39)=2.3, p<.03.
limits: Effects are 30-60 ms, with p values near .03-.05. Visual-field methods assume lateral projection. No EEG. Later work (Aihara 2017, the 2024 EEG study) did not find a clean right-only locus.
agent_relevance: This is the root of the right-hemisphere story. It says insight feels like recognising weakly pre-activated candidates. For an agent that suggests generating and holding weak candidates before verifying, not a hemisphere mechanism.

source: Jung-Beeman and Bowden (2000) The right hemisphere maintains solution-related activation for yet-to-be-solved problems. Mem Cognit 28:1231-1241
finding: Backward link for the 2003 paper. After 7 s of effort, solutions were primed more in the left visual field (RH). After only 2 s or 1.25 s of viewing, priming was symmetric. Authors conclude both hemispheres activate the solution at first, but only the RH maintains it.
numbers: Experiments 1A, 1B, 2A, 2B and 3; 7 s vs 2 s effort. In Exp 2A women showed symmetric priming and men a slight lvf-RH advantage. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read. Sex difference and timing dependence show the effect is fragile to procedure.
agent_relevance: Timing matters: held weak activation after long effort. In an agent, persistence of unresolved candidates in a scratch list is the closest analogue.

source: Aihara et al. (2017) Anodal tDCS of the right anterior temporal lobe did not significantly affect verbal insight. PLoS ONE
finding: Within-subjects tDCS over right ATL (two montages) had no significant effect on Japanese RAT or on matchstick arithmetic. Authors say results do not support right ATL as the central locus of insight.
numbers: N = 66 (53 males, 18-44 y), 2 days, active vs sham. RAT bi-cephalic: 7.34 (SD 2.24) active vs 7.75 (1.93) sham correct, p=.43, Hedges g=-0.19 (95% CI -0.69, 0.30). Extra-cephalic montage n=31 (bi-cephalic n=32). Matchstick Type-C response times 65.2 vs 91.4 s (p=.41). Hard Type-B matchstick: only 3 solvers overall, so inconclusive for non-verbal insight.
limits: Japanese kanji RAT with distractors is not the English CRA. Power was low for the hard matchstick items. Conventional large-pad tDCS is not focal. Montage and task differ from Chi and Snyder, so it is not an exact replication. CI of g spans about -0.7 to +0.3, so small positive effects are not excluded.
agent_relevance: Causal claim for a single hemisphere site is not safe. Do not build agent mechanisms on right-temporal specificity.

source: Salvi et al. (2020) tDCS to the right anterior temporal lobe facilitates insight problem-solving. Sci Rep 10:946
finding: High-definition tDCS over right ATL raised CRA solutions overall and by insight, compared with pre-stimulation, sham, and left frontopolar stimulation. Authors discuss that the earlier within-subject replication (Aihara) failed and blame poor focality and task.
numbers: Three groups of N=36 (108 after 11 exclusions). Group effect F(2,107)=3.64, p=.03, partial eta2=.064; group x time F(4,214)=3.23, p=.01, partial eta2=.057. Solving style x group F(2,107)=3.15, p=.015.
limits: Sham is a separate group, so sham comparison is between-subjects. Many post-hoc tests (18 listed). One author (Beeman) is from the founding lab line. One task (CRA).
agent_relevance: Supports a modest causal role for right ATL in CRA only, but with small effects and not independent of the founding lab. Treat as mixed evidence with Aihara.

source: Santarnecchi et al. (2019) Gamma tACS over the temporal lobe increases the occurrence of Eureka! moments. Sci Rep 9:5778
finding: 40 Hz tACS over right temporal lobe raised CRA accuracy versus sham and 10 Hz. 10 Hz tACS did nothing. EEG after stimulation showed more gamma power over both temporal lobes. No effect on rebus puzzles. Independent lab; the closest causal test of the gamma idea.
numbers: N = 31 (30 right-handed). Sham CRA accuracy 8.25 correct (SD 2.8, 55%); 63% of those by insight. 40 Hz vs sham t(30)=3.54 p<.01; 40 Hz vs 10 Hz t(30)=3.17 p<.010; CRA-specific t(30)=5.98; rebus t(30)=0.49. Reported ANCOVA F(2,28)=4.75 with p<0.001, which does not fit that F value.
limits: Some reported p values look inconsistent with their statistics. Gamma-specific entrainment unproven; authors admit noise injection is possible. It tests stimulation, not a pre-solution burst. Within-subject, N=31.
agent_relevance: If real, gamma at right temporal sites aids remote association. No agent analogue. Do not cite as replication of the burst timing.

source: Ghani, Luft, Ovadio-Caro, Muller and Bhattacharya (2024) The receptive brain: up-regulated right temporal alpha oscillation boosting Aha! Creativity Research Journal
finding: Real-time EEG gating: hints given when right temporal alpha was spontaneously high produced more Aha reports than hints given when it was low. Alpha-gamma phase-amplitude coupling at hint time was inversely related to insight reports (as summarised in the paper).
numbers: About 70 sessions of 100 RAT trials; n=17 per condition (19 in a beta control). Insight reports: frequency x session F(1,32)=4.87, p=.035; alpha-up session M=27.11 insight reports, planned contrast p=.017. Overall insights main effect of frequency F(1,32)=8.99, p=.005, partial eta2=.22.
limits: Authors list N=17 per condition as low. Right temporal site only was tested. Causality not shown. Insight is self-report. Hint-timing manipulation, not a solution burst.
agent_relevance: Real-time brain-state gating is an actual online signal in humans but needs EEG. The model analogue is timing hints or reconsideration to a high-uncertainty state (see d10, d11).

source: Dynamic signatures of the Eureka effect: an EEG study. Cerebral Cortex (2023) (author list not recorded)
finding: Failure to find gamma. In a perceptual Eureka task (blurred scenes), the Eureka condition showed higher alpha and theta coherence mostly in the right hemisphere, lower beta power over parietal and central areas, lower alpha power over frontal and occipital areas and lower right fractal dimension. Gamma and theta power showed no significant difference.
numbers: 29 recruited, 25 analysed (age 25.2 +/- 4.0), plus 10-person pilot. Cluster-based permutation test, cluster-forming p<0.05, about 18.9% of trials discarded to equalise counts. Bands: theta 4-7, alpha 8-12, beta 13-30, gamma 31-100 Hz.
limits: Perceptual recognition, not verbal CRA or riddles, so it is a boundary test, not a direct failed replication. Corrected (cluster) statistics were used. N=25.
agent_relevance: Right-lateralised alpha and theta coherence but no gamma power effect. Partial support for the right hemisphere and against a general gamma signature. No use for a model.

source: Gwak, Son and Kim (2026) Revisiting the Uniform Information Density Hypothesis in LLM Reasoning (arXiv 2510.06953v3)
finding: Per-step entropy profiles separate correct from incorrect reasoning. Correct traces show smooth downward entropy; incorrect traces show noisy entropy with unresolved sharp spikes. Choosing the most locally smooth trace improved accuracy. So an entropy spike goes with errors, not with correct answers.
numbers: Math (AIME2025, BRUMO2025, HMMT2025, MinervaMath) with Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill models; reported gains up to 32% relative over vanilla accuracy; +33% AIME2025, +4% BRUMO, +25% HMMT, +3% Minerva (as printed); non-math (GPQA-D, LSAT) relative gains 5-13%. Qwen3 mean accuracy 0.35 / 0.65 / 0.67 for 1.7B / 4B / 8B.
limits: Math and exams, small open models, no RAT or riddles. Gains are selection among sampled traces (best-of-N style), so compute is not matched to a single sample. Measures uncertainty of text steps, not a sudden jump just before the answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no evidence found that a late entropy or confidence jump predicts correctness on insight items; existing evidence points the other way. A cheap selection signal is smooth entropy. Test against plain best-of-N and self-consistency at equal tokens.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514 v2): scope and limits
finding: Re-read for the scope gaps. Only small open families (Qwen2.5, Llama) were GRPO-tuned; domains were math, crosswords and spatial puzzles (Rush Hour). Mid-reasoning shifts are rare, do not grow with training, and seldom help. Forcing a reconsideration under high entropy improved accuracy across cues; on MATH, forced reconsideration gave +5.97 pp for Qwen2.5-7B but -4.19 pp for Llama 3.1-8B (a subset).
numbers: 1M+ traces, hundreds of checkpoints, three domains. Authors state results are limited to tasks with well-defined correctness signals and a small set of families. They note existing metrics misclassify hesitations as insight at up to 30% in some settings.
limits: No closed or frontier models, no insight-type tasks (riddles, RAT, matchstick). Gaps 3 and 5 remain open. The paper says whether the pattern holds for open-ended reasoning is open.
agent_relevance: Entropy-gated reconsideration is a ready design to test at equal tokens on insight items. Do not assume the Llama result transfers; its sign flips by model.

source: Fascendini, McGregor, Gupta and Griffiths (2026) The Riddle Riddle: testing flexible reasoning in LLMs and humans (arXiv 2606.27103)
finding: Reverse insight test. Riddles rewritten so a literal answer is right. LLMs scored much higher on genuine riddles than on riddle riddles. Humans did the opposite. LLM mistakes were mostly over-inventive reasoning.
numbers: Nine frontier LLMs and 100 humans. LLMs 84.9% on genuine riddles vs 50.7% on riddle riddles; humans 50.5% vs 80.5%. 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles came from inappropriate inventive reasoning; 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles came from overextended literal reasoning.
limits: Abstract and setup read; the model list and prompts were not tabulated. Authors suggest retrieval of memorised riddles explains LLM strength. Strategy-selection test, not neural.
agent_relevance: Boundary: an insight-style step (restructure, decoy listing) can hurt when the problem is literal. A fixation-break operator should be gated by a check that the literal reading failed.

source: Anonymous (2025) The NazoNazo Benchmark / Metacognitive Bottleneck (arXiv 2509.14704): re-read for verification
finding: Verification failure means a correct candidate sits in the thought log but is not endorsed. It accounts for 5-39% of a model's wrong answers. The paper only suggests fixes (better calibration, structured verification, stopping rules); it did not test an independent checker model.
numbers: 201 riddles, 38 models, human mean 52.9% (n=126). Non-reasoning 7.6%, reasoning 17.6% (c05; abstract re-read).
limits: Detection is by string match in logs, so it may over- or under-count. Gap 8 is untested here.
agent_relevance: A candidate-list-then-judge step is the obvious test. Run an independent checker on the candidate list at equal tokens.

source: Kounios et al. (2006) insight-label rate and the problem-vs-style question (gap 7 context)
finding: Human insight labels are about 56% of solutions in both experiments, but participants decide the label, and any one problem can be solved either way. The authors say classification by problem type is not definitive.
numbers: Insight share 56.2% (SD 8.3) in Exp 1 and 55.8% (SD 13.9) in Exp 2; noninsight 42.5% and 43.4%. Between-subject SDs of 8 and 14 points show large individual style differences.
limits: This source gives no figure for labels on errors; the 22.7% (SD 16.4) of incorrect trials is from the 2024 EEG study (a16). Same source as d01/d02 for counting purposes.
agent_relevance: Insight rate of 55-56% mixes problem and style. Treat Aha rate as a style variable, not a quality measure. Do not train or score an agent on Aha-like words.

source: Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments (J Intell, Sep 2026) (author list not recorded)
finding: Aha ratings may be inferred judgments (called JOAs) rather than reads of restructuring. In spatial move puzzles, Aha ratings were highest for solutions where the first move was correct, not for ones needing a representation change. Stronger growth mindset linked correct first moves to Aha.
numbers: N=377 introductory psychology students (mean age 18.80, 68% female), 4 problems, 3 min each.
limits: Online survey, spatial puzzles, students, correlational. Not verbal or EEG. Bears on gap 7: the label follows correctness and style, not just restructuring.
agent_relevance: Do not treat Aha-like text in a trace as proof of restructuring. Score outcomes, not feelings.

source: Comparing Aha! moments in problem solving and generative ideation (J Intell, Aug 2026) (author list not recorded)
finding: Aha strength did not differ between CRA or polysemous-associate solutions and category generation responses. In generation, later responses were more likely to be aha responses, with longer pauses and more novelty.
numbers: 64 participants analysed after exclusions; two-step procedure: aha yes/no, then strength rating.
limits: Self-report. N=64. No neural data. Supports that Aha tracks retrieval dynamics (slow, late, novel) and not a special solving mode.
agent_relevance: Late, slow, novel candidates feel like Aha. For an agent, allow late generation of remote candidates and then verify.

source: Kounios and Beeman (2009) The Aha! Moment: the cognitive neuroscience of insight. Curr Dir Psychol Sci 18:210-216
finding: Not opened. Full text could not be retrieved (publisher page not readable by curl; not in PMC). It reviews Jung-Beeman 2004, Kounios 2006 and 2008, whose numbers are in the primary papers opened here and by the cross-checker.
limits: Unopened. Gap 6 is closed for Bowden and Jung-Beeman 2003 and Kounios 2006 only, not for the 2009 review.
